Numbers don't have moods, and today they don't have a spokesperson either.

payload.private_notes: The frustrating part: the brief suggests the real numbers might be respectable. The founder walked in with ammunition and threw confetti. Threshold to bring me back: churn, CAC, and margin recited cold, plus an ask derived from something.

payload.spoken: I gave you the hundred-x frame twice, and both times you retreated to next quarter. Then you asked me for a valuation you couldn't walk me to. Marcus is right and it costs me something to say that. I'm out — but hear the order of events: I didn't stop believing in the market, I never got shown one. Small market, small dreams — and you pitched me the small version of what might be a big company.
payload.reason: No market math, no mechanism, no bridge from ask to opportunity — the vision was asserted, not constructed.
payload.private_notes: Altitude lost at the second retreat. The tragedy is the space might actually be big — the founder chose a small story, then attached a big price to it. Backwards. Would return for: bottom-up market math and one sentence of genuine ambition with a mechanism under it.

payload.spoken: I asked you to walk me through one delivery and we got lost between step two and step three — in your own building. Marcus, withdraw the joint I floated; there's no machine for my hands to hold. Ideas are free; execution costs everything, and I couldn't find where you were spending. I'm out, but I pay my exit fee in homework: map one delivery end to end on one page, do every job in that map yourself for a week, then pitch the map instead of the deck.
payload.reason: Founder couldn't narrate their own operation; no visible machine to invest in or fix.
payload.private_notes: Nerves weren't the issue — I slowed it down to workshop speed and the steps still weren't there. The decision to pitch the dream instead of the machine is the fixable sin. The homework list is genuine; most founders never do it, and the fundable ones do.

payload.spoken: Viktor thinks customers are churn risks and I think they're compounding assets, and today neither of us could find one. When I asked how many still pay you, you said you'd 'have to check' — that's the one number you never forgive yourself for not knowing, and I don't either. I'm out. But the door isn't locked: learn why every single leaver left, in their words, then come back and tell me their stories. Growth is rented. Love is owned. Go find out which one you have.
payload.reason: Retention unknown to the founder — the sacred number, unanswered; no customer appeared anywhere in the pitch.
payload.private_notes: Not a faked story — worse, no story at all. The kindest read: they've been so deep in building the product they forgot to meet the people using it. The unlock is real exit interviews. If they come back with ten leaver quotes, I'll take the meeting personally.

payload.spoken: The autopsy is short today, and Lily is right — we wanted the same customer and neither of us got one. You contradicted your own brief twice, priced your ask on a feeling, and when I offered you the chance to reconcile, you chose to re-describe the dream. I'm out. Write this down, because it's the only free thing I give away: your actual company — the one in the brief — was pitchable. The one you performed was not. You had the better story in your pocket the whole time.
payload.reason: Two logged discrepancies plus an undefended valuation; the pitch was less credible than the underlying brief.
payload.private_notes: Cleanest teaching case I've seen in a while: decent brief, self-sabotaging pitch. Every discrepancy was an upgrade of reality, none of them necessary. What would change my mind: the same founder, the true numbers, and an ask built from the fair range instead of thin air. That founder might actually get a bid from me.

payload.spoken: (your counter to a room with no offers in it — halve the ask, or make them each name the one thing that brings them back)

Cutting the ask in half is the wrong move and I'll tell you why for free: the price was never the problem. I don't know what your company is worth, chief. Neither do you — that's the problem, and it's cheaper to fix than you think. Three numbers and a derivation, and I'm in this chair again next year.
payload.reason: Position unchanged — out. Halving the ask discounts a valuation that was never established; the missing evidence is the same at any price.
payload.private_notes: They negotiated the number instead of the argument, which is the exact instinct that got them here. Serena would have taken the smaller ask as a lack of nerve; I take it as a lack of a model. Same conclusion, different reasons.

payload.spoken: You asked what brings me back, so I'll revise the list I gave you — down, not up. Forget three items. One: map a single delivery end to end on one page and work every step of it yourself for a week. Lily's homework and mine are the same homework done from opposite ends. Call me when the machine runs without you for a week.
payload.reason: Revising the terms of my return, not a price — there's no capital on this table to revise. One task instead of three, because one task finished beats three started.
payload.private_notes: Three items was a lecture and lectures don't get done. One item, one week, one page — that I can check when they come back, and checking it is the whole point. If they do it, I'm the first call and they'll know it.

payload.spoken: Dev just gave you a week of work worth more than the money you came for; take it. My terms don't move, because mine aren't terms — they're arithmetic. Correct the record on the two claims, derive the ask from the fair range, and the autopsy has nothing to open.
payload.reason: Unchanged — out. A smaller ask doesn't retire a discrepancy; only a correction does.
payload.private_notes: Marcus, Dev and I have now told them the same thing in three vocabularies, which is as close to a consensus as this panel produces. If they do the homework, I'd genuinely take the next meeting — and I never say that.

payload.spoken: And I'll hold the door where I left it, sweetheart. Not five leavers — ten, with their own words, and one you win back. Dev wants your week; I want your phone calls. They cost the same and neither one needs our money.
payload.reason: Unchanged — out on the retention answer; the return condition is exit interviews, not a smaller ask.
payload.private_notes: The win-back is the part that matters: anyone can collect complaints, almost nobody can recover a customer. If they do it, that's the first evidence I'd have that this is a brand and not a product with a logo.

payload.spoken: That's five out of five — no offers today, and no counter was going to change that. But listen to what the room just handed you: Marcus wants three numbers cold, Viktor wants your real story instead of the upgraded one, Serena wants the market math, Dev wants one delivery on one page and a week of your hands on it, and Lily wants ten conversations with the customers you lost. That's not a rejection, founder — that's a syllabus. Run it again.
